food.text: Settlements appeared in Mesoamerica around 3000 BC, and by 2000 BC most of the region was practicing agriculture. Farming had begun around 8000 BC, and the first crops included avocados, beans, chili peppers, gourds and squashes.

As hunter-gatherers in Mesoamerica cultivated wild plants, they built up a surplus of "starvation foods" near their seasonal camps. This surplus could be used when hunting was bad, during droughts, and when resources were low. Over time, dependable crops let people settle permanently.

Maize was domesticated from teosinte, and the change was considered one of the most essential advancements in the history of human life in Central America and Mexico. A single cob of maize could produce much more food than a cob of teosinte.

Chocolate was a drink long before it was a sweet. By 1900 BC on the Pacific coast of Chiapas, the Mokayan people consumed bitter, frothy, watery cacao drinks, making them the earliest known cacao drinkers in the region.
Maize, beans and squash formed a triad of staples in ancient Mesoamerica, commonly called the "Three Sisters". Growing these three crops together helps to retain nutrients in the soil.

Maya cuisine can be traced by archaeological evidence as early as 1500 BC. With maize as a significant and sustainable food source, the Maya expanded their palate and began to cultivate and incorporate many other foods into their diet.
Turkeys and dogs were among the animals domesticated in Mesoamerica. Yet the lack of suitable large animals meant none was developed for transportation or labour.

Mesoamericans eventually settled into a sedentary lifestyle based on plant domestication and cultivation, supplemented with small game hunting. This farming life let permanent settlements grow into villages and opened the way to division of labor and social stratification.

Traces of cacao have been found in bowls and jars dated between 1851 and 1045 BC in the city of Puerto Escondido, Mexico. The decorations on these ceramics suggest that cocoa was a centerpiece of social gatherings among people of high social status.

Ancient Maya diet centered on four domesticated staples: maize, squash, beans and chili peppers. Archaeological evidence suggests that Chapalote-Nal-Tel was the dominant maize species, though others were likely being used too.

Mesoamerican cultivation may have started by accident. Certain plant seeds were eaten and not fully digested, so plants grew wherever human habitation took them. The alternative is that people deliberately brought wild plants closer to a campsite so they were easier to collect.

art.text: At the site of Zohapilco, some of the oldest ceramics in Mesoamerica have been found, dating back almost 5,000 years. The area had a high population and was a clay-rich source for brickmaking.

The aspect of the Olmecs most familiar today is their artwork, and Olmec artworks are considered among the most striking of the pre-Columbian Americas. Offerings ritually deposited at the shrine of El Manatí push the beginnings of Olmec civilization back to at least 1600 to 1500 BC.
Pottery shaped as pots called tecomates has been found at Tlapa and Huamuxtitlán. Because of this ceramic style, we know the region had an early cultural development that predated the Olmecs.
Ceramic figurines found at Zohapilco represent pregnant women and could have influenced the later Olmec civilization. Olmec art shows that the Olmec could have adopted very similar styles of art.
A female ceramic figurine from the Huamuxtitlán valley indicates an archaeological occupation of eastern Guerrero. It is contemporary with the Ocós Phase of Chiapas, dated to 1500 to 1350 BCE.

The appearance of Olmec-type figures at Marquelia on the Costa Chica could prove an Olmec transition process. A similar process has been proposed for Mazatán, Chiapas, during the Cherla and Cuadros Phases, dated 1350 to 1150 BCE.

science.text: Some pre-Columbian cultures in Mesoamerica practised trepanation, the intentional opening of a living person's skull, from at least the mid-Preclassic era, around 1500 BCE. The practice continued in the region until about 1200 CE.

Trepanation was an intentional, planned operation to open or bore into the skull of a living person, using tools specifically designed for the purpose. It could be done by drilling, incising, abrasion, or some combination of these. Its purposes ranged from the medicinal, to relieve pressure or other ailments, to the ritualised and experimental.

Two trepanned skulls from the homelands of the Tlatilco civilization, which flourished around 1400 BCE, suggest the practice has a long tradition. However, the cultural origin of these particular specimens has been disputed.

Trepanation was much less common among Mesoamerican civilizations than among the Andean ones, at least judging from the comparatively few trepanned crania uncovered. The record is complicated by skull mutilation carried out after death to make "trophy skulls" of captives and enemies. Pre-Columbian art sometimes shows rulers adorned with or carrying the modified skulls of defeated enemies, or the ritual display of sacrificial victims. Several Mesoamerican cultures used a skull-rack, the tzompantli, on which skulls were impaled in rows or columns of wooden stakes.

Evidence for Mesoamerican trepanation comes from several kinds of sources. These include physical skull remains from pre-Columbian burials, allusions in iconographic artworks, and reports from the post-conquest period.

politics.text: San Lorenzo was the first Olmec site to show state-level complexity. It dominated the Gulf Coast lowlands and spread Olmec culture across the rest of Mesoamerica. It was the largest city in Mesoamerica from roughly 1200 BCE until 900 BCE.

At Paso de la Amada, the oldest known Mesoamerican ballcourt, dated to 1400 BCE, was not placed in a ceremonial center. It stood beside high-status residences, which suggests it was reserved for elite members of society.

Around 1200 BC, modest villages at Nakbe were leveled and filled in to serve as platform foundations for large new buildings. This indicates that platform construction and monumental architecture were planned, simultaneous events.

Mound 6 at Paso de la Amada began as a public meeting house but grew smaller inside while its platform grew larger. Building the platform must have required a large recruited labor force, suggesting a group of leaders or a single ruler directed the work.

Archaeologists divide Olmec history into four stages: Formation (1700 to 1300 BCE), Integration (1300 to 900 BCE), Expansion (900 to 300 BCE) and Disintegration (300 BCE to 200 CE). San Lorenzo rose to the height of its power in the San Lorenzo phase, about 1400 to 1000 BCE.

The Olmec colossal heads were carved from basalt boulders brought from the Sierra de Los Tuxtlas, more than 150 kilometres away. Because moving them took so much human effort and resources, it is thought they portray powerful individual Olmec rulers, each with a distinctive headdress.

At Paso de la Amada, the growing platform of Mound 6 supports the idea that power became more concentrated over time. The governing body appears to have shrunk, and the mound may have been a display of power and prestige, or served practical purposes, or both.

Olmec-style artifacts appear earlier in parts of Guerrero than in the Veracruz-Tabasco area. Objects from the Amuco-Abelino site in Guerrero reveal dates as early as 1530 BC, hinting that Guerrero played an important role in early Olmec culture.

Many words that entered Mayan from a Mixe-Zoquean language relate to prestige concepts and high culture. This indicates that the Middle Preclassic Maya were deeply impressed and influenced by their northwestern Olmec neighbors.

philosophy.text: Mesoamerican calendars, built around a 260-day year, were used in religious observances and social rituals such as divination. The system probably originated with the Olmecs. A settlement already existed at Izapa in southeast Chiapas before 1200 BCE.

Rubber balls found at El Manatí in a freshwater spring were buried with other ritual offerings. Five of them date to about 1700 to 1600 BC. This suggests the Mesoamerican ballgame had religious and ritual meaning even at this very early date.

The Olmecs appear to have practiced ritual bloodletting, drawing their own blood as part of ceremony. The archaeological record has no explicit picture of it, but numerous natural and ceramic stingray spikes and maguey thorns have been found at Olmec sites, and certain artifacts have been identified as bloodletters. Bloodletting and the Mesoamerican ballgame both became hallmarks of nearly all later Mesoamerican societies. The Olmec civilization flourished from roughly 1200 to 400 BC.

Izapa lies at a latitude of about 15° N, where the Sun passes through zenith twice a year. There are 260 days between those zenithal passages, matching the length of the sacred calendar. Gnomons, used to watch the Sun's path, were found at this and other sites.

El Manatí is a sacrificial bog with artifacts dating to 1600 BCE or earlier. It holds the earliest evidence for Olmec culture. Sedentary farmers had lived in the area for centuries before San Lorenzo grew into a regional center.

A dozen rubber balls dating to 1600 BC or earlier were found at El Manatí, a bog 10 km east of San Lorenzo Tenochtitlan. They predate the earliest known ballcourt, at Paso de la Amada, from about 1400 BC. Still, it is not certain they were used in the ballgame.

One theory holds that the sacred 260-day almanac was set in motion at Izapa on August 13, 1359 BCE. It rests on the site's astronomy, geography and paleontology. The theory is offered as a possibility only, and the source says the almanac may well have begun then.

culture.text: In the Early Preclassic phase, from 2500 to 1200 BCE, pottery-making spread across the whole of Mesoamerica. Maize and vegetables became well-established crops, and society grew socially stratified. The process ended with the first hierarchical societies along the coast of the Gulf of Mexico.

Around 1800 BCE, the Monte Alto culture of Guatemala's Pacific lowlands produced giant stone heads and potbelly sculptures called barrigones. They were found at Monte Alto near La Democracia, Escuintla.

By 2500 BCE, small settlements were growing in Guatemala's Pacific Lowlands, at places such as Tilapa, La Blanca, Ocós, El Mesak and Ujuxte. Guatemala's oldest ceramic pottery has been found in these villages.
In the early Preclassic period, the Capacha culture was a driving force in the process of civilizing Mesoamerica. Its pottery spread widely across the region, carrying its style well beyond its home.

Around 1500 BCE, the Tlatilco culture emerged in the Valley of Mexico and became one of the principal Mesoamerican population centers of its time. Its people were adept at harnessing the natural resources of Lake Texcoco and at cultivating maize.

From 2000 BCE, archaeologists have documented a heavy concentration of pottery along the Pacific coast of Guatemala. Recent excavations suggest the Highlands were a geographic and temporal bridge between these Early Preclassic coastal villages and the later cities of the Petén lowlands.

Some authors argue that Tlatilco, a major center of the Valley of Mexico, was founded and inhabited by the ancestors of today's Otomi people. If so, a living culture would trace its roots back to this early settlement.

The Preclassic Monte Alto culture and the Olmecs both drew obsidian from the Tajumulco Volcano source in southwest Guatemala. This source was almost forgotten during the Classic and Post Classic periods.
